newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Institute seeks ways to raise world tin demand.
newsitem.headline: Institute seeks ways to raise world tin demand.

text.p: New uses for tin are being studied with the aim of increasing world tin consumption by 20,000 to 30,000 tonnes annually, Rod Bedder, managing director of the International Tin Research Institute, said on Tuesday.
Bedder told the first World Tin Conference organised by the institute that environmental protection laws were making tin an increasingly attractive subsitute for lead.
"There is a marketing push for lead-free (products)," he told the conference, adding that the first lead-free mobile phone, laser printer or colour television would score heavily.
In the motor industry, Bedder noted EU plans to ban lead from all vehicle components, except batteries, by 2002.
Most developed countries insisted on the use of lead-free solders in the plumbing industry, Bedder noted.
Another potentially important use for tin was in the manufacture of hunting cartridges, he said, adding that the first one million pure tin cartridges were sold last season.
The institute was also researching uses for tin in lead acid batteries, glass and in fire-retardant additives for plastic used in cables, aircraft, motor vehicles and furniture.
The tin research institute, created by six major tin producers in 1995, has an income of $3.5 million annually from a production levy provided by its sponsors.
